per_quote.text: The goal of the present research was to examine how political climate moderates the relationship between self-reported political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.
Controlling for age, education, income, and race, there was an interaction between political conservatism and conservative political climate for both vaccine and booster hesitancy
such that liberals were less likely to be hesitant regardless of political climate.
However, conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions.
We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023.
We assessed regional political climate using zip code data provided by participants and 2020 presidential election results sourced from the New York Times [22].

Regression analysis (Table 3) indicated that when controlling for age, education, income, race, and vaccine access, political conservatism and conservative regional climate were positively associated with vaccine hesitancy
As political conservatism increases vaccine hesitancy also increases, but this increase is even greater for individuals who live in a more conservative regional climate.
The interaction for vaccine hesitancy indicates that at the lowest levels of conservatism (i.e., liberalism) vaccine hesitancy is lower regardless of regional climate.
The most conservative participants in liberal climates were 60% likely to get boosted, while conservatives in conservative climates were less than 35% likely to get boosted

Because we used 2020 presidential election votes by zip code as a proxy for political climate, it must be noted that other zip code-based differences could be driving the associations noted in this paper.

the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied.

It remains unclear whether these patterns hold in settings where the student population is predominantly AI and where cultural norms surrounding kinship, community, and identity may differently orient relational processes.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties.

Our selection included a tribal school in one of the most geographically isolated and smallest villages (school A), another larger tribal school in a more populous village (school B), and a private, college preparatory school situated near the largest village in the area (school C).

Reciprocity was strongly positive across all three schools (School A: AME = 0.114, p < 0.001; School B: AME = 0.049, p < 0.001; School C: AME = 0.109, p < 0.001), consistent with the robust reciprocity effects documented in studies of non-AI adolescents [9].
Transitivity (GWESP) was likewise consistently positive (AME = 0.016–0.035, all p < 0.001), reflecting the well-documented tendency for triadic closure in adolescent friendship networks [9,10].
Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.

Sexual orientation homophily was also significant and positive (AME = 0.002–0.028), an understudied pattern that suggests meaningful social stratification along lines of sexual identity even in these small, relatively homogeneous school settings.
Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample.

the network structure of these AI adolescents is powerfully shaped by universal endogenous processes (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic commonalities (gender, grade, sexual orientation). Substance use and depression show negligible associations with friendship tie formation
Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.
a single, simultaneous observation of the network and of individual attributes cannot capture changes in network formation and behavior over time.

cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time

By focusing on reservation schools, where AI youth are the norm rather than a statistical minority, this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research and contributes new insights into the unique architecture of AI adolescent social worlds.
